proxy_language: Proto-Chibchan (reconstructed), with Muisca (Mosca/Chibcha) as the best-attested Chibchan language of the Colombian Andes; Timote-Cuica as a Venezuelan Andean peripheral comparandum
proxy_rationale: Abriense (Abrigo/Tequendama rockshelters, c. 12,000-8,000 BP, Sabana de Bogota), Tequendamense and El Jobo (Pleistocene-early Holocene points, Falcon, Venezuela) are known only from lithics and faunal remains; no language can be linked to them directly. A Pleistocene gap of 8,000+ years separates them from any reconstructible language. The most defensible regional proxy is the Chibchan family (Colombian highlands, Isthmo-Colombian area), with Muisca as the only well-documented Andean Chibchan language (colonial grammars by Lugo 1619 and the Quesada vocabulary). Chibchan is a convenience proxy, not a claim of ancestry; Timote-Cuica (Venezuelan Andes, poorly attested, possibly Chibchan-related) offers a second weak anchor. El Jobo in coastal Venezuela is even less linkable.
phonology: Muisca (as recorded in colonial orthography, interpreted with caution): stops p t k (plus labialized kw/qu), b d g appear in spelling but may be allophonic or Spanish-influenced; affricates ts, ch, tz (c-hacek like), fricatives s, z, sh-like (written x), h; nasals m n, plus ny (ñ); liquids l, r; glides w, y; vowels a e i o u plus a high central vowel written as ie, y or u-dot (often transcribed ɨ). Proto-Chibchan (Constenla Umana 1981, Pache 2018): *p *t *k *kw *ts *s *h *m *n *l *r *w *y, vowels *a *e *i *o *u plus *ɨ; contrastive nasal vowels in several daughters; no reliable tone reconstruction. Voicing contrast in stops is uncertain for Proto-Chibchan.
phonotactics: Mostly open or lightly closed syllables: (C)V(C), with CV the dominant shape. Muisca roots are commonly CV, CVC, CVCV (e.g. chie, bosa, gue, sua). Codas are limited, mainly n, s, k, l or a glide; word-final vowels are very common. Consonant clusters are rare inside roots; sequences arise at morpheme boundaries and are often broken or simplified. Initial clusters are not attested. No tone; stress is likely penultimate or root-initial but is not reflected in spelling.
orthography: Use a simple Latinized transliteration modelled on scholarly Muisca/Chibchan conventions: p t k b d g, ts, ch, s, z, h, m n, l r, w y, vowels a e i o u, plus i-bar written as y or ie only if needed. Prefer plain ASCII; use no diacritics. The apostrophe is not a Muisca convention; avoid glottal-stop marks. Write names lowercase with single spaces between words; capitalize only for presentation.
morphology: Muisca is agglutinating and largely suffixing, with some prefixes. Verbs take pronominal prefixes (z- or a- 1st, m- 2nd, a- or Ø 3rd) and suffixes for tense, mood and plural. Nouns have no gender or classes; plurality is optional (suffix -ky, -ngi in some sources). Possessive/genitive is shown by juxtaposition or the possessive prefixes (za- my, mu- your, ni- his or her). Chibchan languages in general show postpositions, a case-like suffix system (-ka locative, -a/-ngi dative-ish) and SOV order. Derivational patterns include nominalizers (-ca, -qua 'place of, instrument', -n, -s) and agent-type forms; reduplication is limited (mainly intensifying or plural in some roots). Treat all of this as approximate: Muisca documentation is thin and Proto-Chibchan morphology is only partly reconstructed.
compounding: Compounds are head-final: modifier + head (noun-noun with possessor first), mirroring Muisca juxtaposition, e.g. 'water + mother' types seen in toponyms and theonyms such as Bachue (Fucha-chigua). 'X of Y' is Y + X by juxtaposition (possessor before possessed), optionally with the locative/relational suffix -ka on the possessor. Instrument or place nouns are formed with a verbal or nominal root plus -qua ('place/thing of', as in many Muisca place names such as -quira/-qua). Agent names ('Y-maker') are Y + verb root + nominalizer. Linkers are generally absent; avoid hyphens between parts or keep them minimal.
noun_phrase_order: Possessor before possessed; modifier (adjective) usually follows the noun in Muisca, though descriptive compounds also appear modifier-first. Numerals and demonstratives are poorly documented. For game purposes: possessor + head for genitives, noun + adjective for attributive phrases, head-final for compounds.

notes: Speculative proxy: the cultures are archaeologically known only from lithic and faunal remains, and the language link to Chibchan is a regional convenience, not a documented ancestry. Muisca spellings in the colonial sources are inconsistent (Spanish orthography, uncertain voicing, the central vowel written variously), so forms here are normalized and some glosses carry real uncertainty; the roots marked reconstructed are tentative Proto-Chibchan comparisons. The suggested names are ASCII-only and avoid apostrophes and glottal marks, which the Muisca record does not support (the current game names with ' are unsound). No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word, since this language is not Goidelic.
